vignette: Two years ago, Margot Vance was traveling with a humanitarian delegation through a volatile border region when the landscape turned to chaos. She had arrived in a quiet Arab village, seeking to deliver medical supplies, but the calm shattered when militants set fire to the outskirts. Margot watched as thatched roofs erupted into towering flames, the heat pressing against her skin as smoke choked the narrow alleys. Amid the panicked flight of residents, she found herself trapped near a burning structure, desperately shouting directions to a group of displaced families while trying to shield a young child from falling debris. The stress was absolute, a suffocating weight that left her feeling utterly powerless. Even though the crisis eventually passed and the families were evacuated, the image of the flames and the sounds of their desperate calls were seared into her mind. Those sensory fragments now lived inside her with terrifying fidelity; when she closed her eyes, she did not see ordinary dreams but relived the moment as if it were unfolding again. The memories felt more real than normal, so vivid that the heat and acrid smoke seemed to coat her throat whenever the past intruded without warning. The boundary between then and now began to dissolve quickly, and the triggers she encountered in daily life directly shaped her internal landscape. Encountering those triggers, like a sudden flare of stress or a distant visual of flames, would immediately drive her to throw herself into work or tasks to keep her mind occupied. At the same time, the sight of geographic tension or fire would instantly amplify her threat sensitivity, making her feel threatened by strangers approaching her even in ordinary situations. Whenever the trigger of ethnic or environmental tension resurfaced, it would harden her conviction that she should have protected others and that she failed, while the comparison that somebody else would not have gotten into this situation would follow, leaving her not sure her life was worth living anymore. These crushing appraisals did not stay contained; they pulled the fragmented recollections deeper into her consciousness, making the memories feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things. When the memories intruded, so vivid that she was suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, she would instinctively work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts. The rawness of those recalled moments directly fueled her fear, turning ordinary proximity into perceived danger until she found herself repeatedly checking that doors and windows were locked. As the memories looped back into her mind, the self-recrimination would intensify, feeding the belief that life was not worth living and reinforcing the weight of her failure. Because the memories could be triggered without warning by any ambient cue, everyday environments became minefields, and the auditory recall of the event would instantly transform neutral stimuli into potent triggers. Over the following months, this cycle tightened relentlessly within her data science career. The exhausting state of constant threat forced her into further avoidance, as she would throw herself into work or tasks to keep her mind occupied rather than face the alarm. Her hypervigilance and the compulsion to repeatedly check that doors and windows were locked kept her scanning the environment, which only widened her trigger list and made stress or visual flames feel more inevitable. Throwing herself into work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts ultimately backfired, because the mental fatigue and forced pauses would allow the memories to return more frequently and vividly. The relentless pace of overworking drained her capacity to regulate, making her more reactive to stress and turning minor sensory shifts into full triggers. This cycle of avoidance and rumination never truly reduced the danger; instead, the chronic mental strain from going over and over why the event happened to her only deepened her sense of threat from strangers and environmental cues. Her husband, David, noticed the quiet distance settling over their home; she had come to believe that engaging with the world was too dangerous, and her relentless schedule left her emotionally absent even on their anniversary. The occupational consequences were undeniable: deadlines slipped, and her team relied on her less as her isolation deepened. Now, at forty, Margot sits in a therapist's office with a heavy, exhausted clarity. She knows the loop is closing around her, though she has never named it. The sight of a campfire at a friend's barbecue still sends her pulse racing, and the geographic tension she once felt in border regions now simmers in any crowded urban space. She seeks help because the weight of not sure her life is worth living anymore has become impossible to carry alone, and because she is most afraid that the very strategies meant to protect her are the ones eroding her marriage and her career. She hopes to find a way to step out from under the shadow of the flames without losing the people who remain, even as she fears that stepping forward might mean finally feeling everything she has spent two years running from.
